The Kazakh-steppe group is the Yueban (Battle of Ikh Bayan page), a different polity. Corrected to the Dzungaria-Barkol remnant; Yiwu itself is carried by ledger 119 (gain) and 126 (loss), not by the baseline.

correction.text: the Huyan King's remnant in Dzungaria and the Barkol side of the Hami circle, to its last mention in 151; Yiwu (Hami, 100 km) is Han again from 126 (ledger)

keyframe_review.note: As for 106: the Huyan King's branch 'continued to resist' after 126 and 'was last mentioned' attacking Yiwu in 151, in eastern Dzungaria, not the Ili. Corrected to the same remnant without Yiwu, which Ban Yong's subjugation took in 126 (ledger 126); the state ends in 151, two years before Cliopatria's 153.

region.text: the Xiongnu homeland north of the Qin wall, before the Donghu conquest

ledger.note: 209 BCE: Modu kills Touman and makes himself chanyu. 'He came to power by ordering his men to kill his father in 209 BCE' (Modu Chanyu page); Touman reigned 220-209 BCE (Xiongnu page). The Xiongnu already held the plateau under Touman; the empire is dated from Modu. Cliopatria's first shape begins in 208.

region.text: the Donghu of eastern Mongolia and eastern Inner Mongolia, west of the Liao River

ledger.note: 208 BCE: the Donghu are destroyed. 'By 208 BCE, the Donghu had been defeated'; their remnants split into the Xianbei and Wuhuan (Modu Chanyu page). The Xiongnu page places the Donghu in 'eastern Mongolia and Manchuria'. The Donghu have no Cliopatria row. [fx-02, 2026-11-01: region narrowed from Eastern Mongolia plus Greater Manchuria to Eastern Mongolia plus eastern Inner Mongolia, without Jilin, Heilongjiang, Outer Manchuria and Liaodong: the Modu Chanyu page (opened 2026-11-01) says 'The eastern border stretched as far as the Liao River' and 'By 208 BCE, the Donghu had been defeated'.]

region.text: the Donghu country not held by the donghu dossier's shape: the steppe of eastern Mongolia and eastern Inner Mongolia up to the Liao River

ledger.note: 208 BCE: the rest of the Donghu country. 'By 208 BCE, the Donghu had been defeated and their remnants split into the Xianbei and Wuhuan tribes'; 'The eastern border stretched as far as the Liao River' (Modu Chanyu page, opened 2026-11-01). The donghu dossier's shape (north Hebei, south-eastern Inner Mongolia, west Liaoning) is far smaller than the Xiongnu shape's eastern reach, so the Donghu gain above moved only the cells the donghu dossier holds and the compiler had to snap 5,089 cells onto the keyframe in -208 (finding F061); this event takes the remainder of the Donghu country from nobody. The year is the page's 208; the extent is Cliopatria's Xiongnu shape of 208 east of the homeland, cut at the Liao River.

region.text: the original Xiongnu homeland on the Yellow River: 'Modu also retook the original homeland of Xiongnu on the Yellow River'

ledger.note: c. 203 BCE: Modu retakes the Ordos that Meng Tian took in 215 BCE. The Xiongnu page says Modu 'retook the original homeland of Xiongnu on the Yellow River' but gives no year, and neither the Modu Chanyu page nor the Meng Tian page (opened for this revision; it says only that the Qin collapsed 'three years after his death', which it puts in 210 BCE) dates it. The counterpart is nobody: Cliopatria's Qin row ends in 209 and the Han start in 202, so no Qin or Han force stood on the Ordos in 203. The year is Cliopatria's (its shape extends south in 203, the year Modu also 'defeated' the Yuezhi), not the page's: confidence 1.

region.text: the Hexi Corridor between Dunhuang and Qilian

ledger.note: 203 BCE: the Xiongnu seize a large part of the Yuezhi land. In the second war the Xiongnu 'seized a large area of the territory originally belonging to the Yuezhi' (Yuezhi page, 203); Modu 'defeat[ed] the Yuezhi in 203 BCE' (Modu Chanyu page). Cliopatria's 203 shape already contains 0.18 of the Hexi Corridor's 0.21 M km2, but the Yuezhi page keeps their homeland 'between Dunhuang and Qilian' until the Xiongnu 'drove them from the Hexi Corridor' in 176, so 203-176 is drawn as contested (mirrors yuezhi.json /ledger/1).

region.text: 'the Yuezhi and Wusun in Gansu and the Tarim Basin': the Xinjiang part of the Yuezhi homeland, mostly the Tarim Basin

ledger.note: 178 BCE: the Tarim passes from the Yuezhi to the Xiongnu. 'In 178 BCE, the Xiongnu overran the Yuezhi and Wusun in Gansu and the Tarim Basin' (Modu Chanyu page). This is the same land that yuezhi.json /ledger/2 records as a loss to the Xiongnu; the oases then paid tribute rather than becoming Xiongnu land, so the next event draws it as vassal tint. The year is the page's; the extent (the Xinjiang part of Cliopatria's Yuezhi shape) is the researcher's reading.

region.text: the Tarim Basin and the eastern oases: 'the Yuezhi and Wusun in Gansu and the Tarim Basin'

ledger.note: 178 BCE: the Xiongnu overrun the Tarim. 'In 178 BCE, the Xiongnu overran the Yuezhi and Wusun in Gansu and the Tarim Basin' (Modu Chanyu page); the Laoshang Chanyu page dates the same conquest to 164 BCE. The oasis states paid tribute rather than becoming Xiongnu land: vassal tint.

region.text: the steppe north of the Tian Shan (Dzungaria) and the Altai and upper Irtysh country that Cliopatria adds between 197 and 170 BCE, beyond the oases and Hexi

ledger.note: c. 178 BCE: the westward growth beyond the oases. Between its 197 and 170 BCE shapes Cliopatria adds 0.89 M km2: 0.36 M km2 are the Tarim and Turfan-Hami (the two events above and below) and 0.53 M km2 (Dzungaria 0.34, the Altai and upper Irtysh 0.18) are pasture that no page opened names. The Modu Chanyu page gives only the westward conquest of 178 BCE ('overran the Yuezhi and Wusun in Gansu and the Tarim Basin') and an undated extent ('the western borders of the empire reached the Pamir Mountains'); the Laoshang page has the Xiongnu 'driving out the Yuezhi and Sakas' in 164 BCE; the Wusun page puts the Wusun in Gansu, and the Yuezhi page only a scholars' guess of a Yuezhi homeland 'in the grasslands to the north of the Tian Shan'. No page places a state in Dzungaria in 178, so the counterpart is nobody. Confidence 1: year and land are the researcher's bridge.

region.text: the Hexi Corridor

ledger.note: 176 BCE: the Xiongnu drive the Yuezhi from the Hexi Corridor, ending the contest that began in 203 (mirrors yuezhi.json /ledger/3). 'drove their western neighbour Yuezhi from the Hexi Corridor in year 176 BC' (Xiongnu page).

region.text: the Hexi Corridor

ledger.note: 176 BCE: the Yuezhi are driven from the Hexi Corridor. 'In 176 BC, when the Xiongnu drove them from the Hexi Corridor and killed their king' (Xiongnu page); the Laoshang Chanyu page gives '177 or 176 BCE' and the skull cup; the Yuezhi page 'Circa 176 BCE'. The Wusun of Hexi 'resettled in Gansu as Xiongnu vassals' (Wusun page, c. 162 BCE).

region.text: the Ili valley, 'immediately north of the Tian Shan mountains'

ledger.note: 132 BCE: the Wusun, Xiongnu vassals, take the Ili. 'In 132 BC the Wusun, in alliance with the Xiongnu,' drove the Yuezhi from the Ili valley (Yuezhi page); 'Liejiaomi attacked the Yuezhi in the Ili Valley, and the Wusun settled the area' c. 133-132 BCE (Wusun page). Cliopatria's 144 BCE shape already reaches the Ili.

region.text: the Ordos region; Wuyuan and Shuofang commanderies

ledger.note: 127 BCE: Wei Qing retakes the Ordos for Han. 'In 127 BC, General Wei Qing invaded and retook full control of the Ordos region'; 'Two commanderies were established in the region; Wuyuan and Shuofang' (Han-Xiongnu War page). Mayi (133) and the raid of late 129 BCE preceded it without taking ground.

region.text: the steppe south of the Gobi, between the Han frontier and the desert

ledger.note: 124 BCE: Han armies push into the steppe. 'Han expeditions went into Mongolia in 124 BC, 123 BC, and 119 BC'; 'In early 123 BC, General Wei Qing set off to Mongolia with an army to attack the Xiongnu' (Han-Xiongnu War page).

region.text: the Yanzhi and Qilian mountain ranges; the Hunye King's land

ledger.note: 121 BCE: Huo Qubing takes the Hexi Corridor. 'General Huo Qubing led light cavalry through five Xiongnu kingdoms, taking the Yanzhi and Qilian mountain ranges from the Xiongnu'; 'the Hunye King and 40,000 Xiongnu soldiers surrendered'. 'By 115 BC, the Han had set up commanderies at Jiuquan and Wuwei'; Zhangye and Dunhuang followed the defeat of a Qiang-Xiongnu force in 111 BCE (Han-Xiongnu War page).

region.text: the Donghu land of eastern Mongolia and Manchuria, the Wuhuan's: 'the eastern wing of the Xiongnu'

ledger.note: 121 BCE: the Wuhuan leave Xiongnu rule and the eastern grasslands are dropped. 'Until 121 BC, the Wuhuan were a tributary of the Xiongnu empire'; 'In 121 BC, the Han dynasty general Huo Qubing defeated the eastern wing of the Xiongnu. He then settled the Wuhuan in five commanderies' (Shanggu, Yuyang, Youbeiping, Liaoxi, Liaodong) on the northern Chinese border (Wuhuan page). The land beyond 114 E (1.4 M km2 of the 126 BCE shape that the 110 BCE one lacks) is the Donghu land of 208 BCE (ledger); the Wuhuan moved into Han commanderies and no state took it. The year is the page's; the page names no land, so the extent is the researcher's reading.

region.text: the steppe south of the Gobi

ledger.note: 119 BCE: the Battle of Mobei (January-June) ends the fight for the land south of the Gobi. Han 'besieged and captured the Fortress of Zhao Xin in the Orkhon Valley'; Huo Qubing 'reached as far as Lake Baikal' (Battle of Mobei page). 'There was a true truce ... for seven years, which ended after a Xiongnu raid in 112 BC.'

region.text: the steppe south of the Gobi; the chanyu's court withdraws north of the desert

ledger.note: 119 BCE: the Xiongnu court is driven north of the Gobi. The Xiongnu 'had to hole up in the cold, barren land of the northern Gobi Desert and Siberia' (Battle of Mobei page); the chanyu was 'forced ... to flee north of the Gobi Desert' (Han-Xiongnu War page). Han did not settle the Gobi-south steppe, so the land goes to nobody. The eastern grasslands beyond 114 E that Cliopatria also drops are the 121 BCE event above (Wuhuan page).

region.text: the Ili valley

ledger.note: c. 115 BCE at the latest: the Wusun break with the Xiongnu. 'When the Xiongnu ruler died, Liejiaomi refused to serve the Xiongnu. The Xiongnu then sent a force against the Wusun but were defeated' (undated); the Wusun 'subsequently took over the Ili Valley, expanding over a large area and trying to keep away from the Xiongnu', and Zhang Qian was sent to the Wusun 'in 115 BC' to propose an alliance against the Xiongnu (Wusun page, re-read for this revision: it dates the break nowhere). 115 is the latest year the sequence allows, the researcher's bridge.

region.text: the territory of the Luli King of the Right, the Tarim Basin and Cheshi

ledger.note: 72 BCE: the Han-Wusun campaign. 'In 72 BC, the joint forces of the Wusun and Han invaded the territory of the Luli King of the Right' (Han-Xiongnu War page); the Wusun page: 'an army of 160,000 men' that 'captured the Tarim Basin and Cheshi'. The Xiongnu page says 'around 80 BC, the Xiongnu attacked the Wusun in a punitive campaign'.

region.text: the Turfan Depression (a 100 km disc round Turpan)

ledger.note: 67 BCE: Han takes Turfan. 'In 67 BC, the Han empire gained absolute control over the Turfan Depression' (Han-Xiongnu War page). [fx-02, 2026-11-01: region narrowed from the whole Turfan-Hami box to a 100 km disc round Turpan, as the page names only the Turfan Depression; mirrors han-dynasty ledger/35. Page re-opened: 'In 67 BC, the Han empire gained absolute control over the Turfan Depression'.]

region.text: the Western Regions: the Tarim Basin and the eastern oases

ledger.note: 60 BCE: the Rizhu King surrenders and the Tarim passes to Han. 'in 60 BC, the Rizhu King surrendered to Protector General Zheng Ji,' after which 'the Han imperial court established the Protectorate of the Western Regions' (Han-Xiongnu War page); the Protectorate page dates the post to 59 or 60 BCE with its seat at Wulei.

region.text: the Tarim Basin and the western steppe

ledger.note: 60 BCE: the Protectorate of the Western Regions ends the fight for the Tarim and the west. Zheng Ji 'was commissioned as protector-general of both the Northern and Southern routes' with 'a general headquarters at Wulei'; 'In 51 BCE ... the Wusun nation was brought under Han submission' (Protectorate page).

region.text: the steppe north of the Gobi, the chanyu's court

ledger.note: 56 BCE: Hutuwusi revolts as Zhizhi Chanyu. 'In 56 BCE Hutuwusi, elder brother of Huhanye, revolted, called himself Zhizhi Chanyu' (Zhizhi Chanyu page); the Xiongnu page counts five claimants in 58-54 BCE (Tuqi dead 56, Runzhen killed by Zhizhi 54). Rebel dossier zhizhi-xiongnu.

region.text: Huhanye's Xiongnu, the whole remaining state

ledger.note: 53 BCE: Huhanye submits to Han. 'Huhanye moved south and submitted to the Chinese' and sent his son Shuloujutang as hostage; he 'visited Chang'an for the Lunar New Year' of 51 BCE (Xiongnu page); 'In 53 BC, Huhanye decided to do so and surrendered to Han empire rule' (Han-Xiongnu War page). Tributary status, lighter tint; Cliopatria's alliance row runs 50 BCE-13 CE.

region.text: the steppe north of the Gobi

ledger.note: 49 BCE: Zhizhi abandons the Orkhon for the north-west. He 'successfully fought the Wusun', 'gained control of the Dingling' and 'made his capital in the lands of the Jiankun' (Zhizhi Chanyu page), leaving the steppe north of the Gobi to Huhanye.

region.text: the lands of the Jiankun and the Dingling

ledger.note: 49 BCE: the Siberian north goes to Zhizhi. In 49 BCE 'He successfully fought the Wusun, gained control of the Dingling and made his capital in the lands of the Jiankun', who 'may have been the Yenisei Kirghiz' (Zhizhi Chanyu page); Modu had conquered 'the Dingling of southern Siberia' (Xiongnu page, undated). Cliopatria drops the land north of 52.25 N from 66 BCE; the 66 and 50 BCE keyframes now keep it to this year (0.33 M km2 in Khakassia, Tuva and Transbaikal), so that keyframe and ledger agree.

region.text: the whole Xiongnu state

ledger.note: 10 CE: Wang Mang's Xin breaks with the Xiongnu. 'In 9 AD, the Han official Wang Mang usurped the Han throne'; 'During the winter of 10 and 11 AD, Wang amassed 300,000 troops along the northern frontier' (Han-Xiongnu War page); the Xiongnu page: in 24 CE Huduershi 'talked about reversing the tributary system'. Cliopatria's alliance row ends 13 CE.

region.text: the Western Regions

ledger.note: c. 23 CE: the Xiongnu regain the Western Regions. 'The Xiongnu had taken advantage of the situation and gained control over the Western Regions' (Han-Xiongnu War page, undated, under the Xin); the protector-general's post 'was abandoned' in 8-22 CE and the eighteen states asked in vain for its return in 45 CE (Protectorate page). The year is the end of the Xin, the researcher's bridge. The Protectorate page, re-read for this revision, says only that the post 'was abandoned after the usurpation of Wang Mang (Xin dynasty) from 8 to 22 CE' and does not mention the Xiongnu; the year stays the researcher's bridge.

region.text: Bi's power base in the south: eight tribes with 40,000-50,000 men

ledger.note: 48 CE: the Southern Xiongnu secede. 'In 48 AD, a confederation of eight Xiongnu tribes in Bi's power base in the south ... seceded from Punu's kingdom and acclaimed Bi as chanyu'; Bi submitted to Han in 50 CE, his court was set at Meiji County, Xihe Commandery, and his followers 'resettled in eight frontier commanderies' (Xiongnu page). The rump 'around the Orkhon' under Punu is the Northern Xiongnu, continued in this dossier. Cliopatria's shape changes in 51.

region.text: Yiwu and Lake Barkol (Pulei)

ledger.note: 73 CE: Dou Gu's expedition reaches Lake Barkol. 'In 73 AD, General Dou Gu ... advanced towards the Northern Xiongnu, defeating the Northern Xiongnu' and pursued them to Lake Barkol (Han-Xiongnu War page); 'Dou Gu and Geng Chong led a great expedition in the Tarim Basin ... Han withdrew in 75' (Xiongnu page).

region.text: the Western Regions

ledger.note: 74 CE: Han retakes Turfan. 'In 74 AD, Dou Gu retook Turfan from the Xiongnu' (Han-Xiongnu War page); the protector-general's post was re-awarded in 74 (Protectorate page).

region.text: Hami (Yiwu) and Turfan

ledger.note: 77 CE: Han withdraws from Hami. 'the Han garrison at Hami was forced to withdraw in 77 AD, which was not reestablished until 91 AD' (Han-Xiongnu War page); 'Han withdrew in 75' (Xiongnu page). Xiongnu influence returns to the northern oases while Ban Chao holds the south (73-102).

region.text: the Northern Xiongnu heartland on the plateau

ledger.note: 87 CE: the Xianbei kill the chanyu. 'In 87 AD the Xianbei defeated the Northern Xiongnu and killed chanyu Youliu', taking his skin as a trophy (Xiongnu page).

region.text: from the Altai to the Khangai Mountains

ledger.note: June 89: Dou Xian's expedition. 'a major expedition launched against the Northern Xiongnu by the Han dynasty in June 89 AD' from Jilu, Manyi and Guyang with the Southern Xiongnu as allies; it 'defeated the Northern Chanyu at the Altai Mountains and pursued them westwards', 'killed 13,000 Xiongnu troops and accepted the surrender of 200,000 Xiongnu from 81 tribes'; late in 89 Dou Xian 'carved the cliff Inscription of Yanran' in the Khangai (Battle of Ikh Bayan page).

region.text: the Northern Xiongnu heartland on the plateau

ledger.note: 91: the Xianbei war ends with the Northern chanyu's flight. 'In 91, the Northern Xiongnu were defeated by the Han dynasty and the Xianbei began occupying the Mongolian Plateau, absorbing 100,000 Xiongnu tribes' (Xianbei page); the Xiongnu page has 'the Northern Chanyu fled with his followers to the northwest, and was not seen again' and the scattered Northern Xiongnu 'absorbed by the Xianbei' (undated). The year is the page's; the extent is the researcher's reading.

region.text: Hami (Yiwu) and Turfan

ledger.note: 91: Han re-establishes Hami and the protectorate. The Hami garrison 'was not reestablished until 91 AD' (Han-Xiongnu War page); 'Ban Chao was made protector-general and reconquered the Western Regions' in 91 (Protectorate page).

region.text: the Mongolian plateau east of the Altai

ledger.note: 91: the plateau passes to the Xianbei. 'the Xianbei began occupying the Mongolian Plateau, absorbing 100,000 Xiongnu tribes' (Xianbei page, 91, no month); 'After another Han attack in 91, the Northern Chanyu fled with his followers to the northwest, and was not seen again' (Xiongnu page). 'Some Xiongnu remained in Dzungaria near Lake Barkol, and a new chanyu was installed'; he was killed in 93 and 'no Northern chanyu is recorded after him' (Battle of Ikh Bayan page). The Xianbei dossier should carry the gain.

region.text: from the Altai to the Khangai Mountains

ledger.note: February 91: the last Han pursuit. Geng Kui and Ren Shang, advancing from Juyan, 'defeated the Northern Xiongnu ruler' and captured his mother, killed 5,000 of his troops and 'drove him west from Altayn Nuruu. He was not heard from again' (Battle of Ikh Bayan page).

94: Fenghou is acclaimed chanyu of the remnant. 'Surrendered Northern Xiongnu rebelled and acclaimed Fenghou as chanyu, fleeing outside the border'; 'About 10,000 returned to Han' in 96 (Xiongnu page). The dossier continues as the Northern Xiongnu remnant in Dzungaria; Yuchujian, the last chanyu of the old line, had been killed in 93.

region.text: Yiwu

ledger.note: 119: the remnants capture Yiwu. 'Remnants captured Yiwu' in alliance with the Nearer Jushi Kingdom (Xiongnu page); Fenghou had 'surrendered with about 100 followers' in 118. The keyframes for 91-153 leave Yiwu (Hami, 100 km) out of the baseline, so this event and the loss in 126 carry it.

region.text: Yiwu

ledger.note: 126: Ban Yong subjugates the remnants. 'Ban Yong subjugated them. A Huyan King branch continued to resist' (Xiongnu page); the Protectorate page has Ban Yong restoring the protectorate in 123-124.

region.text: Pulei (Barkol), the Huyan King's base, with the Dzungarian remnant; Yiwu itself had been Han since 126

ledger.note: 151: the Huyan King, last of the Northern Xiongnu, is driven from Yiwu and disappears from the record. 'The Huyan King was last mentioned, attacking Yiwu' in 151 (Xiongnu page); 'a 4,000-strong Han militia defeated the Northern Xiongnu in 151 AD, after which they disappeared from historical records' (Han-Xiongnu War page). The Yueban remnant had moved to the Kazakh steppe (Battle of Ikh Bayan page); the infobox lists the Xianbei, Han, Rouran and Türks among successors.

wars.name: Xiongnu conquest of the Donghu
wars.outcome: Xiongnu victory: 'By 208 BCE, the Donghu had been defeated'; the remnants became the Xianbei and Wuhuan.

wars.name: Xiongnu–Yuezhi wars

zones.text: the Hexi Corridor between Dunhuang and Qilian

wars.outcome: Xiongnu victory: the Yuezhi defeated in 203 BCE, overrun in 178 BCE, driven from Hexi in 176 BCE with their king killed; the Wusun became Xiongnu vassals.
wars.note: The Yuezhi page counts three wars (under Touman, in 203 BCE, and 'before or in 176 BCE'); the Laoshang page dates the skull cup to 177 or 176 and a Tarim campaign to 164 BCE.

wars.name: Battle of Baideng
wars.outcome: Xiongnu victory without territorial change: Gaozu besieged at Baideng (Datong) in the winter of 200 BCE; the heqin treaty of 198 BCE gave the chanyu a Han princess and gifts with 'equal status, and a boundary wall', renewed nine times to 135 BCE.

wars.name: Han–Xiongnu War

zones.text: the Yanzhi and Qilian mountain ranges
the steppe south of the Gobi
from the Altai to the Khangai (89-91 CE)

wars.outcome: Han victory: 'Establishment of Han suzerainty in the Western Regions'; the Ordos (127 BCE), Hexi (121 BCE) and the Tarim (60 BCE) lost, the chanyu driven north of the Gobi (119 BCE), Huhanye a Han tributary (53 BCE), the Southern Xiongnu Han vassals (50 CE) and the Northern Xiongnu destroyed at the Altai (89-91 CE).
wars.note: Infobox dates '133 BC – 89 AD' and '90–91 AD (punitive campaign)'. The Battle of Mobei (January-June 119 BCE, Orkhon valley) and the Battle of the Altai Mountains (June 89) have their own pages, cited in the ledger.

wars.name: Xiongnu civil war of the five chanyus

zones.text: the steppe north of the Gobi
the lands of the Jiankun and the Dingling

wars.outcome: Huhanye prevails with Han support after submitting in 53 BCE; Zhizhi takes the north-west in 49 BCE, moves to Kangju in 44 BCE and is killed at the Battle of Zhizhi in 36 BCE.
wars.note: 'a Xiongnu civil war broke out in 57 BC over the succession' (Han-Xiongnu War page); claimants Tuqi (dead 56), Runzhen (killed 54), Huhanye and Zhizhi (Xiongnu page).

wars.name: Xianbei–Northern Xiongnu war

zones.text: the Northern Xiongnu heartland on the plateau

wars.outcome: Xianbei victory: chanyu Youliu killed in 87; after the Han campaigns of 89-91 the scattered Northern Xiongnu were 'absorbed by the Xianbei' and the plateau passed to them.
wars.note: The Xianbei page dates the occupation of the plateau to 91 ('the Xianbei began occupying the Mongolian Plateau'); 93 is the death of the last Northern chanyu of the old line.

certainty.note: Steppe frontiers throughout; the one sharp line is the Han frontier along the Qin and Han walls ('a boundary wall' in the 198 BCE heqin terms), and the Hexi and Ordos commandery borders after 127-111 BCE belong to the Han dossier.

notes:
Written by the ia-01-a research agent on 2026-10-18 from the pages listed (nine distinct articles for the Xiongnu's budget of nine; two redirects). Revised the same day after review (Meng Tian, Wuhuan, Xianbei and Li Guangli opened for the repair, and the Modu, Laoshang, Wusun, Yuezhi, Zhizhi and Protectorate pages re-read).

Southern Xiongnu (Q188836 shared): the Southern Xiongnu of 48 CE are a different state, a Han vassal settled in the eight frontier commanderies with its court at Meiji in Xihe, so this dossier keeps cliopatria_names ['Xiongnu'] only and records the 48 CE secession as a split; the Northern Xiongnu, 'the rump kingdom under Punu, around the Orkhon', continue this dossier. The Southern Xiongnu dossier (another ia-01 part) should list xiongnu as predecessor and carry the 50 CE vassal_start to Han; Cliopatria's second alliance row (30..105) belongs to it, not to the Northern Xiongnu, who never submitted.
